title: Mohnish Pabrai at Annual Morningstar India Conference on October 24, 2018
summary: Pabrai presents his '10 Commandments of Investment Management': no skimming fees off the top, no investing team, accept being wrong a third of the time, hunt hidden P/E-of-1 stocks like Rain Industries, never use Excel, keep a rope out of the deepest well, be singularly focused like Arjuna, never short, never borrow short and lend long, and be a shameless cloner. The Q&A covers his Buffett lunch and the inner scorecard, concentration, growth versus value, margin of safety, India as an arbitrage on understanding, and his cash policy.

ideas.idea: Thou shalt not skim off the top: use the Buffett partnership fee structure of zero management fee, a 6% hurdle and a quarter of profits above it with a high watermark.
ideas.detail: Performance-only fees stop managers from becoming asset-gathering machines, encourage concentration and cut frivolous expenses; a fund operation, like a steel mill or airline, deserves no guaranteed income if it does not perform.

ideas.idea: Thou shalt not have an investing team: Buffett manages over $200 billion of investments with no analysts, so a fund needs only about half a human to find three or four stocks a year.
ideas.detail: He routinely sees funds with under 100-200 crores and several people hovering around; not collecting fees on assets automatically makes you careful about spending.

ideas.idea: Thou shalt accept being wrong at least one third of the time, per John Templeton, because forecasting a business 5-10 years out is inherently uncertain.
ideas.detail: Being wrong does not always mean losing money; even with a 40% error rate you hit the ball out of the park, unlike brain surgery where even a 0.4% error rate fails.

ideas.idea: Thou shalt look for hidden P/E-of-1 stocks, where next year's earnings roughly equal today's market cap; they appear in his portfolio every two or three years.
ideas.detail: In just over 19 years of managing money at least six or seven such stocks showed up. Auction-driven markets routinely misprice; buy when pessimistic and sell when euphoric.

ideas.idea: Rain Industries was a hidden P/E of 1: bought in 2015 at 30-45 rupees with a $180-200 million market cap on $2 billion of revenue, and by 2018 it earns about 35-50 rupees a year.
ideas.detail: It traded at 10-15x trailing earnings at a multi-year cyclical low, but market forces were likely to produce very different earnings; the bet was that 2018-19 EPS would exceed the 2015 purchase price. Rain was a tremendous investment in 2015, though he gives no tips on it now.

ideas.idea: Thou shalt never use Excel: if you need a spreadsheet to justify an investment, it should be an automatic pass.
ideas.detail: For Rain he needed only the fingers of one hand: a $200 million company that will earn $200 million will not stay priced at $200 million.

ideas.idea: Thou shalt always have a rope to climb out of the deepest well, a lesson from his serially bankrupt, levered entrepreneur father who paid an astrologer for rosy forecasts.
ideas.detail: From the 2007 peak to March 2009 his portfolio fell about 70%, from $600 million to under $200 million with a $675 million high watermark; he broke the Excel rule and modeled end-2010/2011 values showing $1 billion or more to get out of the well. Without leverage, turbulence is survivable.

ideas.idea: Thou shalt be singularly focused like Arjuna: ignore rates, crude, currency, IL&FS or NBFC noise and see only the eye of the fish.
ideas.detail: Brent forecasts swung from $200 to $76 around the Khashoggi affair; none of it matters versus whether a $200 million market cap company will earn $200 million. Find businesses in your circle of competence available at a quarter or less of value.

ideas.idea: Thou shalt never short: the maximum upside is a double and the maximum downside is bankruptcy, with unlimited capital calls.
ideas.detail: He has never shorted and expects to go to his grave without doing so; Buffett and Munger say they were right on hundreds of short candidates but wrong on timing almost every time.

ideas.idea: Neither a short-term borrower nor a long-term lender be: India's testosterone-fueled NBFCs borrowed short and lent long for fat spreads and ran out of confidence before running out of money.
ideas.detail: Buffett's rephrasing of Polonius in Hamlet; levered financial institutions usually go bust from a liquidity mismatch even when assets are solid. To finish first, you have to first finish.

ideas.idea: Thou shalt be a shameless cloner is the tenth and favorite commandment.
ideas.detail: He gives his email so listeners can send him P/E-of-1 ideas, and cloned Buffett's charity-lunch auction for Dakshana.

ideas.idea: The biggest takeaway from the $650,000 Buffett lunch was the inner scorecard: would you rather be the world's best lover known as the worst, or the worst known as the best?
ideas.detail: He bid only to thank Buffett for intellectual property used without IP fees; Buffett aims to make each winner feel they got a bargain, stayed all afternoon for 54 questions, and told his daughters the most important decision is whom you marry. Everything about Buffett and Munger is public domain, but the lunch calibrated what mattered most to him.

ideas.idea: Mutual funds with 50-150 positions and 70-80% annual turnover are like one-night stands; most investors should just own a broad index.
ideas.detail: Businesses take years to reach fair value. In his own concentrated funds a bet is ideally at least 10%, and the top five or six stocks are 70% or more of the pie; holding 25 stocks makes no sense for a stock picker.

ideas.idea: Growth and value are joined at the hip; the ideal investment is a growing pie bought without paying up.
ideas.detail: You do well buying static assets at a huge discount but far better with a growing pie. Of about 200 Indian listed CEOs he met, Chaand Sehgal of Motherson Sumi is among the best, but it is an amazing business at a not-so-amazing price, so he has not invested.

ideas.idea: Margin of safety is the free lunch: buying a dollar for 20-40 cents lowers the odds of loss and raises the upside at the same time.
ideas.detail: Like the Miller commercial, it tastes great and is less filling; there are few free lunches in investing.

ideas.idea: Ben Graham made most of his money owning GEICO, a great business, not from net-nets, and would write a different book today.
ideas.detail: Security Analysis (1934, 1940) came out when markets were drowning in net-nets after the Depression; between undervalued non-growing assets and paying a little for significant growth, you almost always do better with the latter. His unreasonable eleventh commandment is growth at a P/E of 1.

ideas.idea: Performance-only fees do not cause excessive risk-taking when the manager is the largest investor in the fund and never shorts, levers or uses derivatives.
ideas.detail: Dumb investing would hit him twice, through his own net worth and lost future fees; every dollar investors gave him in 1999 is now about $14-15 after fees, always by protecting the downside.

ideas.idea: India offers an arbitrage on understanding: management teams explain their businesses poorly, so investors willing to dig in are in the minority.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Most of the Indian market is still overheated even after corrections, but in some cases there is a large delta between a business's future and what the stock price bakes in, as with Rain in 2015.

ideas.idea: He holds about 10% cash on roughly $800 million, and that last 10% is very expensive capital reserved for ideas that can return north of 40% a year, a 5-6x in five years.
ideas.detail: He will not deploy the final tranche for a mere double.

ideas.idea: Reread Poor Charlie's Almanack every year and work through the 150-plus hours of Berkshire annual meeting videos at buffett.cnbc.com.
ideas.detail: He listens for 30 minutes daily via a waterproof shower speaker, starting from 1994 and reaching 2003 so far; Bad Blood on Theranos is recommended entertainment.

ideas.idea: Auctioning lunch with himself for the Dakshana Foundation, cloned from Buffett, has run seven or eight years starting at 1 cent with no reserve.
ideas.detail: The eBay auction is usually run in November; the lunch can be in any Indian metro or in California or New York, and has brought incredible people out of the woodwork.
